subject: Culture
title: Eid Gifts and Charity
description: A quick win: understand Eid Gifts and Charity.

hook.text: On Eid al-Fitr, children receive 'Eidi'—cash gifts from every elder relative. It's their annual payday.

buildup.text: Eid marks the end of Ramadan. Gifts celebrate the discipline of fasting and the joy of community reunion.

discovery.text: Zakat al-Fitr is mandatory charity before Eid prayer—enough food to feed one person for a day, given per family member.

twist.text: The charity must arrive BEFORE Eid prayer. Late donations count as regular charity, not the sacred obligation.

climax.text: Eid gifting ensures even the poorest celebrate. The system builds redistribution into the holiday's structure.

punchline.text: True celebration includes everyone at the table.

quiz.question: When must Zakat al-Fitr be given?

details.summary: Eid celebrations combine gift-giving with mandatory charity (zakat al-fitr) — Muslims must give to the poor before Eid prayers. Children receive new clothes, sweets, and money.
details.whyItMatters: Eid's combination of personal gift-giving and mandated charity reveals how Islam embeds wealth redistribution into celebration, making generosity both a personal joy and a religious obligation.
takeaways: Zakat al-fitr is mandatory charity given before Eid al-Fitr prayers
Eid gifting includes new clothes, money, and sweets for children
Eid al-Adha involves animal sacrifice with meat shared among the poor

faq.question: What is zakat al-fitr?
faq.answer: Zakat al-fitr is a mandatory charitable gift given by every Muslim who can afford it before Eid al-Fitr prayers. It is typically equivalent to the cost of one meal per family member.

faq.question: How does Eid gift-giving differ from Christmas?
faq.answer: Eid gift-giving is less commercialized than Christmas and focuses primarily on children and the needy. There is no equivalent of Santa Claus or gift-wrapping traditions. Gifts are typically cash, new clothes, and sweets rather than wrapped presents.
